beats.care: The Security Council decides on wars, sanctions and peacekeeping. A seat gives India a louder voice on terrorism, trade routes and tech.
beats.what: India and Tajikistan are both running for the single Asia-Pacific seat on the UN Security Council for 2028 and 2029.
beats.why: Usually a region agrees on one candidate. This time there's a real contest, which an analysis in The Hindu calls a test for India.

cards.body: It's the UN's most powerful body, with 15 members. Five are permanent and hold a veto: the US, China, Russia, the UK and France. Ten are elected for two-year terms, and its decisions bind every UN member.
cards.title: what is the security council?

cards.body: The most recent was 2021–22. Tajikistan has never had a seat.
cards.caption: India's past terms on the Council

cards.body: India hasn't always won these races: it lost contested votes to Pakistan in 1975 and to Japan in 1996.

a.body: Defeating a first-time candidate could dent India's image as a voice for smaller, developing countries.
a.label: Some analysts argue

b.body: India is a top UN peacekeeping contributor and home to about a sixth of humanity, so it has earned the seat.

cards.q: Why is India's 2028–29 UN Council bid tricky?
cards.why: Tajikistan is running for the one Asia-Pacific seat, so India must win two-thirds of the vote instead of walking in unopposed.

cover.label: Share of UN votes needed to win the seat

hook: India has sat on the UN's top table 8 times. *Who's in the way of a 9th?*

learn.t: To win an elected UN Security Council seat, a country needs two-thirds of the votes cast in the 193-member General Assembly.

watch: Rajnath Singh visits Tajikistan's capital Dushanbe for an SCO meeting on 19–20 Oct. The UN vote is in June 2027.
